how: createModelVerifier() builds the model from the overlay spec, derives a scrypt key (N=131072) from the serving credential, HMACs a JSON of spec, model, credential revision and gateway target into a fingerprint, and probes with synthetic text and a synthetic tool schema (15 s deadline, output cap the lesser of 128 tokens and the model limit, fast mode checked twice). The registry PUT must carry verify:true explicitly; slow probes run outside the registry write lock and the store rechecks the stored revision before saving, so a late result cannot undo a delete or another edit.
verevonRelevance: Per-Space model allowlists in Verevon could use the same idea: enablement is a proven fact tied to the credential revision, not an admin toggle.
notes: Quality 4: careful concurrency and fingerprinting (test/model-verification.test.ts); probe cannot certify limits. Does not certify prices, context limits or tool correctness; the doc lists these limits.

name: Document attachments as model input: native provider files, bounded local text fallback, re-authorized every turn
what: Attachments reach the model without a tool call. PDFs and Office files are sent natively where the provider supports them and extracted to text otherwise, with explicit notices for what could not be read, and access to each artifact is rechecked on every turn.
how: loadDocumentInputs() takes the newest attachments first up to 10 documents and 8 MB, authorizes each artifact per turn, dedupes by sha256, name and mime type and emits per-file notices. Fallback extraction runs in a worker thread with a 192 MB heap cap and a 10 s deadline, 200,000 characters per document and 100,000 combined. A route table (OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages and SDK, chat completions, OpenRouter, Gemini and Vertex, OpenCode, gateways, Codex) decides native versus fallback. The tape stores artifact references, not bytes or extracted text, and scanned or encrypted PDFs are reported unreadable rather than guessed.
verevonRelevance: A Space with many members and agents needs one attachment-to-context path that is authorization-rechecked per turn, size-bounded and provider-aware; Verevon's Ingestion or Data plane can own extraction while the Model plane receives references.
notes: Quality 4: bounded, cancellable and re-authorized (test/document-inputs.test.ts, test/orchestrator-documents.test.ts); validated live on several routes per the doc. The doc records live validation across web and Slack with 26 format markers, but states native acceptance for some routes (direct OpenRouter) was not verified.

name: Opt-in backend error reporting that ships unredacted error context to a third party
what: When SENTRY_DSN is set every backend service reports uncaught errors and recorded failures with stacks, cause chains and context, and nothing is scrubbed; performance tracing is optional and manual.
how: initializeErrorReporting() turns default integrations off and enables only uncaught-exception, linked-errors and extra-error-data integrations, with no beforeSend scrubber; reportBackendError() tags error_code and fingerprints by it; SENTRY_TRACES_SAMPLE_RATE adds one http.server transaction per request (named by route template) and one queue.task per terminal run. The docs state events are sent unredacted. History shows the first version was sanitized (#1349) and the later change (#2018) stopped discarding error information so failures can be diagnosed.
verevonRelevance: Verevon must keep ZDR propagation: error and trace sinks must scrub prompts, message text and tool output, so QM's unredacted choice is a negative example unless the sink is operator-owned and in-region.
notes: Quality 2: works and is documented, but removes scrubbing on purpose (test/error-reporting.test.ts). Driven by SPEC's 'Discarded error evidence' lens. QM also keeps an operator error log in Postgres (error_events).

name: Admission gate for synchronous work: pause on handover, nested work admitted, drain awaited
what: A deployment that is handing over background ownership can refuse new synchronous turns, scheduled fires, loop fires and monitor polls with a typed error, while work already admitted keeps running and can be awaited to completion.
how: createAdmittedWork() keeps an AsyncLocalStorage admission context and a set of pending promises; run() rejects with WorkAdmissionClosed when paused or when canStart() says the deployment does not own background work, otherwise tracks the task; nested calls inside admitted work are always allowed; drained() awaits all pending. The API turn path, cron scheduler, loop fire, monitor poller, run worker and every sweeper are wrapped in it; wiring derives canStart from the background-ownership record.
verevonRelevance: A small reusable guard for Verevon blue-green or region moves: one admission function that every long-running entry point passes through makes drain behaviour testable instead of per-subsystem.
notes: Quality 3: small and used by every entry point (test/admitted-work.test.ts). Complements the heartbeat drain and single-owner record in the blue-green record.

name: Per-user server-side UI state with last-writer-wins and a future-skew clamp
what: A person's small UI preferences can be saved on the server so they follow them across devices; the newest client timestamp wins and a client clock far in the future cannot pin the value.
how: GET and PUT /v1/ui-state take a principal id and a key matching ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$, values up to 64 KB, stored in a DurableMap under principal#key; storeUiState() refuses an older updatedAt and returns the stored one; the claimed timestamp is clamped to now plus 5 minutes. The only client use found is the saved inbox filter.
verevonRelevance: The minimum viable cross-device preference sync for Verevon Space shells (sidebar order, pinned rooms, filters) without a sync engine; add per-key versions if conflicts matter.
notes: Quality 2: minimal and tested (test/ui-state-http.test.ts); one use. Qualifies the 'no multi-device engine' record: preferences sync, content is simply refetched. Layout and drafts stay in localStorage.

name: Per-worktree production-shaped dev instance with chat-app pool leases and a delivery canary
what: Any worktree can be booted as a full stack (core, web, portal, optional Slack) on a real model and real Postgres, and every pull request that touches agent or surface behaviour is expected to be exercised there before review.
how: scripts/dev-instance.sh wraps a TypeScript CLI (up, status, down, doctor, canary, restart, logs). A per-slot supervisor restarts crashed children with backoff and probes health every 10 s. Slack Socket Mode is single-owner, so each developer holds a pool of Slack apps leased per slot by an atomic lock; up proves reachability by requiring the app's only socket connection and a canary message that round-trips, rotates past a flagged slot, tears down after 24 idle hours and never steals a slot with a fresh heartbeat. The agent sandbox is local Docker by default, request capture is on, production data is never copied, and a localhost-only portal login bypass is set. AGENTS.md makes this a pre-PR step for substantial changes.
verevonRelevance: A Space needs the same: a one-command stack with a throwaway org, seeded humans and agents and a channel canary so multi-party behaviour can be reviewed before merge.
notes: Quality 4: thorough supervisor with canary and idle teardown (test/dev-supervisor-child.test.ts, test/dev-canary-pick.test.ts); very Slack-specific. The Socket Mode single-owner constraint also explains the single background-owner design in production. Tags (src, docs) agree; this record is mapped to Governance as assurance because the taxonomy has no testing category.

name: Lambda MicroVM agent computer: suspend and resume lifecycle, 7.5-hour rotation and home snapshot to S3
what: On AWS each scope's computer is a Lambda MicroVM with a persistent home: it suspends when idle, resumes on use, is rotated before the platform's 8-hour limit and has its home restored from S3.
how: createMicrovmApi() signs the Lambda microVM REST API (version path 2025-09-09) with SigV4 directly, with image create or update from S3, runMicrovm, suspend, resume, terminate and per-microVM auth tokens. createAwsSandbox() launches with idlePolicy autoResume, 900 s max idle and 3600 s suspended, a 28,800 s maximum duration and rotation after 27,000 s, 4 vCPU, 8 GB memory and 8 GB disk by default, ingress and egress network connectors, a per-scope advisory lock and keyed queue for provisioning, and a durable record per scope. A 90-line HTTP guest daemon (/health, /exec, /write, /read) is the only in-guest component. The profile reports snapshot_to_workspace persistence, process sessions, park on teardown and egress enforcement none.
verevonRelevance: Shows what a managed microVM substrate needs around it (rotation, snapshot-to-object-store, a tiny exec daemon, scope-locked provisioning) if Verevon ever offers per-Space computers on a cloud microVM service.
notes: Quality 3: new substrate with a tested API wrapper (test/aws-microvm-api.test.ts, test/aws-sandbox.test.ts); egress enforcement unavailable. The same guest daemon is reused by the local Docker sandbox image and by published apps on AWS, which keeps behaviour aligned across backends. The service is new (API version 2025-09-09) and no egress enforcement is available through it.

name: Published-app data durability on AWS: Litestream replication with per-deployment STS-scoped S3 prefixes
what: Apps an agent publishes can keep a SQLite database in /data that survives replacement, rollback and microVM loss; the replica is written to S3 with credentials that can touch only that deployment's prefix.
how: createAwsDeployProvider() mints data credentials with STS AssumeRole and an inline session policy limited to s3 object actions under <dataPrefix>/<deploymentId>/litestream plus a prefix-conditioned ListBucket; it stages a litestream config and env into the guest, runs a start script that probes write access, restores the database when a replica exists and the local file does not, and then runs the replicator while tracking live replicator pids; a periodic tar snapshot (default 5 minutes) is the fallback; configuration without both bucket and role fails loudly rather than silently disabling replication.
verevonRelevance: If Spaces host generated mini-apps or pages, per-deployment scoped replication is a cheap durability answer; Verevon should still keep owner data in Data or Application planes and treat app databases as disposable caches.
notes: Quality 3: scoped credentials and loud misconfiguration (test/aws-deploy-provider.test.ts); AWS-only and recent. Fly uses encrypted per-app volumes instead (host-local, not replicated; docs/qa/fly-published-apps.md), and the same document is an acceptance matrix that requires live evidence for isolation, wake and rollback before a provider is approved.

name: Egress enforcement as a typed per-backend capability, with provider policy readback and replace-on-drift
what: Each computer backend declares whether it can enforce outbound limits (none, ip_port or domain); where it can, QM locks the sandbox to the proxy host and verifies the provider actually accepted the policy, and a paused sandbox created under a different policy is destroyed and replaced.
how: EgressEnforcement is part of AgentComputerProfile and effectiveEgressEnforcement() reports none unless core signing and an API base exist. Sprites sets a domain-allow network policy for the proxy hosts and reads it back, throwing on mismatch; E2B (allowOut for the proxy host plus denyOut all traffic), Modal (domain or CIDR outbound allowlist), DigitalOcean (egress allowlist) and smolmachines (allowCidrs with a verified set) combine provider-level allow rules, and E2B, Modal and DigitalOcean also inject HTTPS_PROXY with a per-turn egress token as the proxy password (forceThroughProxyEnv); Porter requires cluster egress restriction (Cilium) and fails sandbox creation closed without it; Superserve applies operator allow and deny rules (not proxy-bound, so its profile still reports none), stamps an egress-policy hash into sandbox metadata and replaces a sandbox whose policy differs; AWS, local Docker and Agent37 report none, and boot only warns about fail-open for the proxy-capable backends when no proxy URL is set.
verevonRelevance: Verevon sandbox leases should expose the same typed enforcement level and refuse or downgrade explicitly; the readback-after-set and replace-on-policy-drift steps are cheap invariants worth copying.
notes: Quality 4: typed capability with readback and drift replacement (test/agent-computer-profile.test.ts, test/sprites-sandbox.test.ts); several backends cannot enforce. Refines the forced-egress record: six backends can lock to the proxy host (Sprites, E2B, Modal, DigitalOcean, smolmachines, Porter), four report none (AWS, local Docker, Agent37, Superserve). Porter sandboxes cannot reach RFC1918 ranges, so the proxy needs an internet-reachable address.

name: Configuration epochs fence stale instances from rewriting newer sandboxes (Superserve backend)
what: During blue-green or rollback, an older core instance cannot recreate or reconfigure a sandbox that a newer configuration already owns; rollback is an explicit, strictly increasing rollout number.
how: createConfigEpochResolver() claims a generation under an advisory lock (one above the highest stored) or takes SUPERSERVE_CONFIG_GENERATION; each sandbox is stamped with its epoch and egress hash in provider metadata; on reconnect a sandbox stamped newer than the instance's epoch is used but marked not current instead of being replaced, and a different egress policy or template replaces the sandbox and its resident files. A name prefix namespaces independent deployments sharing a provider team.
verevonRelevance: Per-Space computers shared across deployment cohorts need the same monotonic fence so a draining cohort cannot overwrite a newer one.
notes: Quality 3: narrow but correct fence (test/superserve-sandbox.test.ts); single backend. Backend-specific; other backends rely on advisory locks and the blue-green owner record.

name: Combined service topology keeps module trust boundaries inside shared workloads
what: Admin runs inside the web workload and the sign-in broker inside the portal workload, so a deployment is three images (core, web, portal) plus an optional egress proxy, but the modules still verify each other as separate services.
how: The CLI folds the admin and auth capabilities into web-ui and portal and rejects conflicting env; the modules keep separate handlers, admin still verifies signed portal identities and forwards them to core which authorizes every privileged action, portal still strips inbound identity headers and checks sessions and CSRF, the embedded broker listens only on 127.0.0.1:8099 and its token and JWKS endpoints stay on loopback. Upgrade rules order web before portal, keep issuer and signing keys unchanged and keep the old workloads at zero capacity for rollback.
verevonRelevance: Verevon can co-deploy small services without collapsing their authority edges; keep every privileged call going through the owner plane.
notes: Quality 3: documented rollout and rollback with embedded boundaries; migration is multi-step. Evidence for the loopback binding is in portal index.ts; the doc and code agree.

name: Rolling-upgrade compatibility rules: immutable migration checksums, import-once legacy routing, dual-readable journals
what: Upgrades are designed so old and new binaries can run against the same database for a while and rollback restores code but never data: migration ids and checksums never change meaning, a mismatch stops the upgrade, and legacy tables are imported once and kept for older readers.
how: docs/upgrading-runtime.md fixes the rules: pin runtime and CLI together, run migrations before serving, qualify the exact candidate against an isolated copy of the database, keep previous images until operational checks pass; sandbox_routing and SANDBOX_SCOPE_BACKENDS are imported once as sandbox records (startup stops if an unconfigured provider is needed); cron_fire_log history is imported into cron_fires and writes from older workers keep importing during the roll; rolling back does not restore database contents, so a recovery point is required for data rollbacks.
verevonRelevance: A checklist for Verevon's Application-plane projections and Space migrations: checksum-immutable steps, import-once with a marker, and an explicit statement that code rollback does not roll data back.
notes: Quality 3: explicit rules that the repo itself partly contradicts in its legacy lens (test/postgres-migration-adoption.test.ts). SPEC's 'Legacy preservation' lens argues against exactly this style of compatibility; the repo does both.

name: Schedule validation that teaches the agent the correct form, and a fire contract with continuity outside the thread
what: A schedule the agent writes is rejected with a message that explains what to use instead (clock-time schedules need cron plus timezone, minimum interval, past start times), and every fire is told it has no memory of earlier fires and where to keep durable state.
how: validateUserSchedule() and the schedule parser throw messages written for the model: everyMs of 24 hours or more is 'a clock-time schedule in disguise' and must use {cron, timezone}; recurring intervals have a 60 s minimum; a past firstFireAt error prints the current epoch to recompute from. renderCronFireInput() wraps each fire with a runtime-context block stating that the thread is fresh, that run state belongs in published Files, how to read the fire log, how to leave a note for the next fire, and (for channel crons with at most 40 members) a roster of mention ids so a reminder actually pings the right person.
verevonRelevance: Agent UX as design rule applied to scheduling: Verevon's Space cron tool should return teachable errors and give each fire a contract for state and mentions.
notes: Quality 3: agent-facing errors and fire contract (test/cron-schedule-guardrails.test.ts); the text is long and model-dependent. Complements the fire-key and authority records; the scheduler also defers busy fires and records outcomes.

name: Memory quality benchmark: replayed conversations scored by a model judge on three axes with floors
what: Memory strategies are compared by replaying canned conversations through extraction and consolidation and scoring the resulting notebook for signal-to-noise, staleness and inference-versus-observation.
how: scripts/memory-bench.ts replays test/memory-bench/conversations/*.json (inference bait, long project arc, noise-heavy debugging, preferences and identity, secrets exclusion, stale-fact supersession) through each strategy kind (per-turn, agent-only) and asks a judge prompt for 0 to 10 scores; DEFAULT_STRATEGY_FLOORS are 5, 4 and 5 and floorFailures() reports misses; it needs a live model key and is run through npm run bench:memory.
verevonRelevance: A ready pattern for evaluating Space memory (room notebooks, agent personal memory): fixed conversations that include a secrets-exclusion and stale-fact case, judged on axes with pass floors.
notes: Quality 3: small but useful (test/memory-bench.test.ts); needs a live model and is not in CI. Not part of CI (needs a live model).

name: Operator bootstrap: CLI-minted five-minute single-use admin login with no account creation
what: After deploying, the operator runs one command that prints a URL which signs in as an already-granted admin once, so the first administrator can reach the console before email or SSO works.
how: qm admin-login seals a token with a key derived from the deployment's PORTAL_SESSION_SECRET under the label portal.admin-login.v1 (exp now plus 300 s, bound to the portal origin and a jti); the portal shows a confirm page, checks the selected email still holds org_admin, and claims the jti once through the core claim store; the command creates no account or role, the grant comes from ADMIN_GRANTS.
verevonRelevance: A break-glass first-admin path for self-hosted Verevon that creates no privilege of its own; Control should keep grants as the only source of authority.
notes: Quality 3: single-use claim enforced (test/admin-login-token.test.ts).

name: Durable-by-default as an engineering rule, backed by a catalogue of process-local-state bugs
what: Anything an operator or the system reads back later (audit, errors, resolved config, queued work, approvals) must live in Postgres; RAM is allowed only as a cache or for disposable state.
how: AGENTS.md states the rule for the blue-green, multi-instance core and SPEC's non-durability lens lists past bugs: a 5,000-event in-memory error ring, scope config in process Maps, Slack approval cards in a Map, completed runs that never enqueued their delivery because it depended on an in-process callback, and webhook in-flight tracking in a process Set (still present on main). In-memory twins exist only as test doubles behind the same interfaces.
verevonRelevance: Adopt as a review lens for Application-plane projections: if a restart or a second instance changes what a user sees, the state is in the wrong place.
notes: Quality 4: a rule with a catalogue of failures; compliance is imperfect (webhook race remains). SPEC admits the webhook in-flight race (qm#1943) is not fixed.

name: Agent-initiated runtime handoff: switch model or harness mid-task and resume with saved tool results
what: The agent can change its own model, harness, reasoning effort or fast mode for the current task or for the scope; the current segment stops and the unfinished task resumes on the new runtime without losing tool results.
how: The runtime tool has get, set and inherit. runtime-control validates the scope, requires a live person for scope-lifetime changes, restricts cron fires to their own task, checks the approved harness and model lists and the person's account route, and refuses changes while a goal is unfinished. A successful change returns terminate:true with a runtimeHandoff in the tool result; the orchestrator loops over segments, adopting each new runtime (at most 8 per task) and recovers the choice from the tape after a crash.
verevonRelevance: Lets a Space agent escalate to a stronger or cheaper model under explicit, auditable rules; Verevon's Model Plane should keep authority over the approved list and cost attribution.
notes: Quality 4: bounded handoffs with recovery from the tape (test/runtime-tool.test.ts); interacts with goals and approvals. Unusual: most products fix the model per conversation or leave switching to the human.

name: Agent-operated deployment runbooks with human-only steps marked and a live release gate
what: Deploying QM is written as a runbook an agent can follow end to end: it collects choices, confirms billing, operates the CLI and cloud tools, and finishes only when a live session canary passes and the administrator can sign in.
how: qm init writes deployment.md, an agent skill and per-provider references; the workflow requires confirming provider identity, region and billable resources before mutation, marks steps only a human can do (linking a cloud account through the vendor's console), and defines done as qm check --live (an authenticated canary that needs a real model reply, persistence and a title) plus admin sign-in and, when requested, a Slack bot reply. The Porter runbook tells an agent to use the vendor CLI and the operator's browser, and to hand the exact URL to the operator otherwise.
verevonRelevance: Self-hosted or sovereign Verevon installs could ship the same agent-operable runbook with a live acceptance gate instead of a long manual.
notes: Quality 3: agent-operable runbooks with a live gate (test/deployment-skill.test.ts); quality depends on the agent.

name: Provider image and template pipelines that bake agent tools into sandboxes
what: Each sandbox provider has a documented way to bake the agent's toolset and the deployment layer into the image so first use does not install packages, with checksums and fallbacks when no baked image exists.
how: E2B builds the template through its Template SDK (qm-base) and can derive a child template with layer tool files baked in; Modal builds a pinned image (uv, requests, openpyxl, AWS CLI v2) and returns an image id to set; DigitalOcean registers a template via a script and otherwise runs on its bare base image with agent none, using a port-forward instead of its REST exec; Superserve templates fix vCPU, memory and disk at build time; layer tools are otherwise converged on first provision after a checksum probe, and the connector SDK bundle is baked outside the home so snapshots cannot hide it.
verevonRelevance: Per-Space computers will need the same baked-image discipline: keep installs out of the first user turn and keep image-installed dependencies outside the snapshotted home.
notes: Quality 3: documented per provider, partly untested here; image drift risk. Docs only for the provider-side steps; the in-repo build scripts exist (scripts/e2b-build-template.ts, scripts/modal-build-image.ts) but were not run.

name: No calls, meetings or calendar in the core product (the calendar tab is a placeholder)
what: QM has no audio, video, huddles, screen share, recording or meeting chat, and its web Calendar view only says coming soon.
how: Greps over src, plugins, desktop and cli for WebRTC, getUserMedia, getDisplayMedia, MediaRecorder, LiveKit, huddle and RTCPeerConnection found only a third-party minified bundle; the desktop shell denies every device permission; plugins/web-ui/src/calendar.ts renders an empty state reading 'Coming soon'.
verevonRelevance: Teams, Slack and Grok Bot lead here; Verevon should not look to QM for meeting features, and should plan meetings as a Channel-plane or Application-plane capability with transcripts feeding Space memory.
notes: Quality 1: negative: no calls, meetings or calendar features. Corrects the scout inventory that listed the calendar tab as shipped; git:03a793fa added the tab but the view body is a stub. Negative result is grep-based.

name: Slack ingress transport: Socket Mode by default, signed HTTP events as an opt-in, both behind the same deferred acknowledgement
what: The Slack adapter connects over Slack's Socket Mode unless the operator asks for HTTP events; either way an event is acknowledged to Slack within a cap and staged durably before handlers run.
how: startSlackPlugin() defaults eventsMode to socket (needs SLACK_APP_TOKEN) and uses an HTTP events receiver only when SLACK_EVENTS_MODE=http with a signing secret and port; both receivers are built from the same staging and acknowledgement-cap options (createDeferredAckReceiver or createHttpEventsReceiver); the CLI secret schema and doctor treat http mode as the special case. Socket Mode connections are single-owner (a second instance on the same app steals half the events), which is one reason production has exactly one background owner at a time.
verevonRelevance: A future Verevon Channel Plane adapter should prefer signed HTTP events (stateless, horizontally scalable) over a single-owner socket, and reuse the ack-after-durable-staging gate.
notes: Quality 3: Socket Mode default is simple and tested (test/slack-http-events.test.ts, test/slack-deferred-ack.test.ts); single-owner socket limits scale. Resolves the scout's open question: the default is Socket Mode, not HTTP.

name: Thin browser client behind a server-side identity holder: no keys or run bearers in the browser
what: The web app is a chat shell whose server process keeps the signed-in identity (HttpOnly cookie or the portal's signed identity header), relays a small set of API routes to core with signed requests, and streams run output over SSE with polling as a fallback.
how: plugins/web-ui/server/index.ts is a node:http server that verifies the portal identity header or reads the HttpOnly session cookie, injects the principal as the turn's actor and proxies about 150 /api route handlers (loops, sessions, deployments, user model auth, crons, skills, runs and run events, projects, keychain, inbox, webhooks, files, memory and more) to core; the browser POSTs /v1/turns?async=1 and watches /api/runs/:id/events; run reads and signals are bound to the verified actor on the core side; model and provider keys, egress and tools stay server-side and the model picker only expresses a preference within the org's policy floor.
verevonRelevance: Matches Verevon's BFF rule (frontend is a UX owner, not an authority): the gateway holds identity and relays typed calls, and the browser never sees credentials or run bearers.
notes: Quality 3: conventional BFF (test/web-ui-body-cap.test.ts, test/web-ui-sse.test.ts); the entrypoint file is overgrown. SPEC calls the web server entrypoint a god file (qm#488): cookies, sign-in, OAuth callbacks, transport and many domains share one module (plugins/web-ui/server/index.ts is large).

name: Installable responsive web app: one build with a phone mode, no service worker
what: Below 860 px the same web build becomes an app-like layout (drawer sidebar, bottom sheets, 44 px touch targets, composer above the on-screen keyboard) and can be added to the home screen, but it has no offline cache or push.
how: PHONE_MAX_WIDTH = 860 is shared by CSS media queries, the composer and the split canvas, which never mounts on a phone; a visualViewport listener keeps the composer above the keyboard; index.html links a manifest that the server generates from the org's brand label; a grep found no service worker.
verevonRelevance: A baseline for Verevon Space on phones: a responsive PWA is cheap, but Teams and Slack set the bar with native push and offline, which QM does not meet.
notes: Quality 3: responsive and installable but without offline or push. No native mobile client exists in the repo.
